agent_judgment.patient_reply:
Thanks for the clear description. Heel pain that is worst with your first steps in the morning and loosens up as you walk is very typical of plantar fasciitis. This is irritation of the thick band of tissue on the bottom of your foot, and it's common when running mileage ramps up. Most people get better with home care, though it can take several weeks to a few months.

What helps:
- Modify training. Cut back mileage and intensity until the pain settles, and avoid hills and speed work for now. Cross-train with cycling or swimming to keep your fitness. Return gradually, increasing weekly mileage by no more than about 10%.
- Stretch daily, especially before your first steps in the morning. Before getting out of bed, pull your toes back toward your shin for 30 seconds, 3 times. Do calf stretches against a wall with the knee straight and then bent, holding 30 seconds each, several times a day.
- Roll and ice. Roll the arch over a frozen water bottle for 10–15 minutes once or twice a day.
- Strengthen. Try towel scrunches with your toes and slow heel raises.
- Wear good footwear. Use supportive, cushioned shoes and avoid going barefoot or wearing flat flip-flops. Replace running shoes with more than 300–500 miles on them. Over-the-counter arch supports or heel cups often help.
- Pain relief. Ibuprofen or naproxen for a short period can help if you have no stomach, kidney or bleeding issues.
- Consider a night splint. It holds your foot flexed overnight and can ease morning pain.

Two quick questions to make sure nothing else is going on:
1. Does the pain get steadily worse the longer you run or stand, rather than easing up, or does it hurt when you squeeze the sides of your heel?
2. Do you have heel pain at night or at rest, swelling or bruising, or numbness, tingling or burning in the foot?

If either is yes, reply and a physician will review. That pattern can point to a stress fracture of the heel bone, which needs an X-ray or other imaging and a different plan. Please also reach out if you can't put weight on the foot, feel a sudden pop or sharp pain, or notice redness, warmth or fever. And let us know if you're not clearly improving after 6–8 weeks of consistent home care. Good luck with the training!
